summary: Defines how PCEP encodes objective functions, which are the optimization criteria used when computing traffic engineering label switched paths, such as minimum cost or widest path. A client can then tell the PCE what kind of best path it wants.

eli5.summary: Directions can aim for shortest, cheapest or widest road. This note defines how to tell the route-planning server which of those goals to pursue.

subtitle: How a PCEP client tells a path computation server what 'best path' means, and how the server says what it supports.

tldr.problem: When a Path Computation Element computes a traffic engineering path, there are many ways to define 'best' (cheapest, least loaded, widest). PCEP had no way to ask for one, or to learn which ones a PCE supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an OF-List TLV in the Open message so a PCE can advertise its objective functions, an OF object in request and reply messages to ask for and report one, and a new RP flag to ask the PCE to say which it used. It defines six objective functions and four new metric types.
tldr.outcome: A client can require or merely prefer an objective function, and a PCE can reject, substitute or report one. Additional objective functions may be defined in other documents.

today: RFC 5541 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5440, and the text points to other work, still in progress when it was written, that defines more objective functions for global concurrent optimization.

sections.title: Why Objective Functions Are Needed
sections.content:
In the Path Computation Element architecture (RFC 4655), a Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths for Traffic Engineered Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) from a network graph and a set of constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) sends it requests. The two talk using PCEP, defined in RFC 5440.

Choosing among candidate paths needs an optimization criterion, called an objective function (OF). Some apply to one request on its own, such as the shortest constrained path using the IGP metric. Others apply to a set of synchronized requests, such as minimizing the aggregate bandwidth consumption of all LSPs. Some optimize a single metric and others a set of metrics.

This RFC extends PCEP so that a PCE can advertise a list of supported objective functions, and so that request and reply messages can carry the objective function. It complements RFC 5440 and defines the six objective functions that RFC 4657 says PCEP must support.
sections.eli5: There is more than one way to pick the best route, like shortest or least crowded. The client and the server need a shared way to say which one they mean.

sections.title: Discovering Supported Objective Functions
sections.content:
A PCE may advertise what it supports using a new optional OF-List TLV, carried in the OPEN object of an Open message during PCEP session setup. The TLV uses the standard PCEP TLV layout: a 2-octet type (4), a 2-octet length and a value. The value is a list of 2-byte OF code points, so the length is N * 2 for N objective functions. The TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the length.

The OF-List TLV MUST NOT appear more than once in an OPEN object. If it does, the session MUST be rejected with error type 1, error value 1 (PCEP session establishment failure, reception of an invalid Open message). If the TLV is absent, that means only that there is no information about supported objective functions. A peer that does not recognize the TLV silently ignores it, as RFC 5440 specifies.

The RFC notes that OSPF and IS-IS based PCE discovery (RFC 5088, RFC 5089) covers only a few generic parameters, while more detailed parameters such as objective functions are better discovered over PCEP itself.
sections.eli5: When two programs first say hello, the route-planner can hand over a list of the goals it knows how to chase. If it hands over no list, the other side just does not know.

sections.title: The OF Object and Where It Goes
sections.content:
The new OF object has Object-Class 21 and Object-Type 1. Its body holds a 2-byte OF Code, a 2-byte Reserved field (set to zero on transmission, ignored on receipt) and optional TLVs that may be defined in the future to carry objective function parameters.

A PCC may include the OF object in a PCReq (path computation request) to say which function it wants. A PCE may include it in a PCRep (reply) to say which function it used, and it may be attached even to a negative reply carrying a NO-PATH object.

Placement matters. For a set of synchronized requests, the OF object MUST come just after the corresponding SVEC object and MUST NOT be repeated for each elementary request. A METRIC object that applies to the whole set follows the SVEC object the same way. For an individual request, the OF object MUST follow the RP object it applies to. The RFC gives updated Reduced BNF for both PCReq and PCRep messages.
sections.eli5: The goal is written on a small card. If the goal is for a whole group of trips, the card goes once at the front of the group. If it is for one trip, it goes with that trip.

sections.title: How a PCE Reacts to a Request
sections.content:
The P bit in the common object header decides how strict the request is. If the P bit is set in the OF object, the objective function is required and the PCE MUST use it. If the P bit is clear, it is only desired: the PCE SHOULD apply it if supported but MAY pick a different one based on local capabilities and policy.

  • OF object unknown or unsupported: follow RFC 5440. With the P bit set, send a PCErr (type 3 or 4) and discard the request. With it clear, the object may be ignored.
  • Function unknown or unsupported, P bit set: send a PCErr with error type 3 or 4 and error value 4, and discard the request. With the P bit clear, the PCE SHOULD apply another (default) function.
  • Function supported but policy forbids it, P bit set: send a PCErr with type 5 (policy violation) and a new error value, 'objective function not allowed'. With the P bit clear, apply another default function.
  • Function supported and allowed: apply it if the P bit is set; otherwise the PCE is free to apply any other.

A new RP object flag, Supply OF on response (bit 24), lets a PCC ask to be told which function was used. If policy permits, the PCE MUST include an OF object in the reply. If not, it MUST send a PCErr with type 5 and the new value 'objective function indication not allowed'. A legacy PCE ignores the unknown flag, and the PCC then decides for itself whether to accept or discard the reply.

If a reply names an objective function the PCC does not recognize, the RFC lists options such as ignoring it and using the path, adding it to its view of the PCE, or discarding the reply and asking again, possibly with the P bit set.
sections.eli5: If the client says 'you must', the server either does it or says no with an error. If the client only says 'please', the server may choose its own goal and, if asked, tell which one it picked.

sections.title: The Six Objective Functions and Four New Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines three functions for a single path and three for a set of synchronized requests. It uses a simple model: a network of N links, a path of K links, a link metric M(L) (IGP metric, TE metric or another), a path cost C(P) that is the sum of its link metrics, a residual bandwidth r(L) and a maximum reservable bandwidth R(L).

  • Single path: Minimum Cost Path (code 1) minimizes C(P). Minimum Load Path (2) minimizes the largest fraction of reserved bandwidth on any link of the path. Maximum residual Bandwidth Path (3) maximizes the smallest residual bandwidth on the path.
  • Synchronized set: Minimize aggregate Bandwidth Consumption (4), Minimize the Load of the most loaded Link (5) and Minimize the Cumulative Cost of a set of paths (6).

For the METRIC object, PCEP already had TE metric, IGP metric and hop count, which apply to one request. This RFC adds four types for a set of synchronized requests: type 4 aggregate bandwidth consumption, type 5 load of the most loaded link, type 6 cumulative IGP cost and type 7 cumulative TE cost. They can bound a result (B bit) or ask for a computation (C bit) in a PCReq, or report a computed metric in a PCRep. The METRIC object follows the SVEC object it applies to. Other objective functions may be defined elsewhere.
sections.eli5: Some goals are about one trip: the cheapest, the least crowded, the widest. Others are about a whole bunch of trips together, like using the least total road.

sections.title: Registries and Code Points
sections.content:
IANA manages a 16-bit "PCE Objective Function" registry shared by the OF object and the OF-List TLV. Code 0 is reserved. Codes 1 through 1023 are assigned by IETF Review, 1024 through 32767 are First Come First Served, and 32768 through 65535 are for Private Use. Codes 1 to 6 are assigned to MCP, MLP, MBP, MBC, MLL and MCC.

The RFC also records the OF object (class 21, type 1), the OF-List TLV (type 4), the RP flag bit 24 and metric types 4 to 7. Two new error values under error type 5 (policy violation) are added: value 3, objective function not allowed, and value 4, OF bit of the RP object set.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps track of which number means which goal, so everybody uses the same numbers. Some number ranges are for sharing and some are for private use.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Nothing here changes message flows or adds new messages, so the PCEP security mechanisms of RFC 5440 still apply and automatically secure the OF object. If a PCEP message is vulnerable, for example because security is not used, the OF object could be part of an attack, but the RFC considers it likely that other objects offer far more significant ways to attack a PCE or PCC.

For management, it MUST be possible to enable or disable objective function discovery and to configure a default objective function. An implementation SHOULD allow a list of authorized objective functions on a PCE. Implementations need not support every function in this RFC.
sections.eli5: The goal card travels in the same locked envelope as everything else, so it gets the same protection. Operators can also decide which goals the server is allowed to follow.
